title: Ang 26–39: Guru Amar Das
hookLine: the third Guru's Sri Rag hymns on the Word and the mind
tomorrow: what do you do when you don't know the way?

lines: HOW DO YOU WASH A MIND?
cards: Washing machines have a setting for almost everything: delicates, heavy duty, a quick rinse. There's no setting for a mind that keeps replaying one conversation at two in the morning. So how do you wash a mind?
Turn to ang twenty-six, and a new voice takes up that exact question.

teach.h: SRI RAG, MAHALA 3: GURU AMAR DAS.
teach.b: The heading reads Sri Rag, Mahala 3: the third Guru, Guru Amar Das. His hymns fill these pages, and they keep coming back to the mind. In paraphrase, the picture goes like this.
The mind gathers dirt, the dirt of haumai, ego, the endless me and mine.
What washes it is the Shabad, the Guru's Word, and the grace of the One. And these hymns name two ways to live: the gurmukh, who faces the Guru, and the manmukh, who follows only their own mind.
Something to tell someone tonight: in these pages, a clean mind isn't an empty one. It's one filled with the Word. Now a neighbor who also starts with the mind.

teach.h: THE DHAMMAPADA: MADE OF OUR THOUGHTS.
teach.b: The Dhammapada, verses of the Buddha, opens this way in Max Müller's English: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts."
Shared ground: both put the mind at the center of a life, and both say it can change.

One honest difference: Guru Amar Das looks to the Guru's Word and the One's grace to do the washing, while the Dhammapada puts the training in a person's own practice, without a creator in the picture.
Two old answers, each in its own words, to the two a.m. question.

how: Guru Amar Das's hymns in Sri Rag stand from ang 26; Sikhs read and sing them in the gurdwara and at home, and turn to Gurbani, the Guru's Word, as the way the mind is washed.

s: Mahala 3 in a heading means Guru Amar Das
the third Guru; his Sri Rag hymns begin on ang 26.
in these hymns, a clean mind is an empty mind
a clean mind is one filled with the Shabad, the Guru's Word.
Guru Amar Das and the Dhammapada say exactly the same thing about the mind
both put the mind at the center; they differ on what does the washing.

games.q: a friend can't stop replaying an argument at two a.m. and asks how Sikhs think about cleaning a mind. what fits Guru Amar Das's Sri Rag?
o: empty it completely: a clean mind is one with nothing in it.
fill it with the Shabad: the Word washes off the dirt of haumai.
push harder: willpower alone is what scrubs a mind clean.
games.why: in these hymns the mind's dirt is haumai, ego, and the Guru's Word, with the One's grace, is what washes it. a clean mind is a full one.

practice: Name one thought that keeps coming back and muddies your mind, and name what usually lets it in: tiredness, a screen, a certain hour.
Then make one small plan for when it returns, like reading a single line of Gurbani, or a slow breath out. Hold the plan quietly while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Ang 26. Where the third Guru, Guru Amar Das, takes up Sri Rag, with hymns on the Word and the mind. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: haumai, literally I-I; ego, the dirt on the mind in Guru Amar Das's hymns.

carryVoice: Your line: the third guru, and a mind the Word can wash. Take it slow.
